title: Syllogisms & Venn Diagrams
relevance: Placement OAs and company logic tests use Venn-based syllogisms, possibility conclusions, either-or pairs, and set counting/min-max overlap questions.

phases.goal: Establish the Venn mappings for categorical statements and the definite-vs-possibility rule.

must_hit.point: All A are B means circle A is drawn entirely inside circle B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate draws A fully nested in B for universal affirmative.

must_hit.point: No A is B means circle A and circle B are disjoint with no overlap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate draws two non-overlapping circles for universal negative.

must_hit.point: Some A are B means the circles overlap; Some A are not B means at least one part of A is outside B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate shows overlap for Some, and an A-outside-B region for Some-not.

must_hit.point: A definite conclusion must hold in every valid diagram; a possibility conclusion holds if it is true in at least one valid diagram.

probes: How do you represent All, No, Some, and Some-not on a Venn diagram, and when is a conclusion definite versus only possible?

hints.1: Think of each category as a circle and how the four statement types place those circles.
hints.2: Map All→nested, No→disjoint, Some→overlap, Some-not→A partly outside B; then separate always-true from can-be-true.
hints.3: Definite = true in every valid diagram; possibility = true in at least one valid diagram.

phases.goal: Show how conclusions follow from nesting, overlap, disjointness, Only a few, and complementary either-or pairs.

must_hit.point: Overlap is bidirectional: Some dogs are birds implies Some birds are dogs, but Some cats are birds need not follow from All cats are dogs and Some dogs are birds.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate keeps Cats inside Dogs, Birds overlapping Dogs optionally missing Cats, and treats the dogs-birds overlap as symmetric.

must_hit.point: Nested All chains force All of the innermost in the outermost, and the innermost region also yields Some of the outermost are the innermost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: For All pens are pencils and All pencils are erasers: both All pens are erasers and Some erasers are pens follow.

must_hit.point: When a set overlaps a region forbidden from another set, the overlapping members are definitely not that other set, but the rest of the set may still meet it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: No tree is a flower + Some trees are fruits ⇒ Some fruits are not flowers, but not No fruit is a flower.

must_hit.point: Only a few A are B means Some A are B and Some A are not B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate translates Only a few engineers are coders into overlap plus a forced engineers-outside-coders region.

must_hit.point: Standard complementary either-or pairs are Some A are B with No A is B, and All A are B with Some A are not B, when neither conclusion is individually definite and they exhaust possibilities.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names those two pairs and requires same subject/predicate plus exhaustive coverage.

must_hit.point: Some A are B and Some A are not B do not form an either-or pair because both can be true at once.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects either-or for Some/Some-not and may answer Neither when neither is definite.

probes: Given All cats are dogs and Some dogs are birds, which of Some cats are birds and Some birds are dogs follows, and why?
When do two conclusions form an either-or complementary pair, and why is Some plus Some-not not such a pair?

hints.1: Sketch the forced regions first, then ask what must be true in every diagram versus only in some.
hints.2: Check symmetry of stated overlaps, nesting for All-chains, and whether undefined pairs are complementary or merely underdetermined.
hints.3: Only II in the cats/dogs/birds case; either-or uses Some↔No or All↔Some-not, never Some↔Some-not.

phases.goal: Contrast definite conclusions with possibility conclusions and true complementary pairs with false either-or pairs.

must_hit.point: Possibility can allow full engulfing of a nested set into an overlap region, but fails if some members are forced into a set disjoint from the target.
must_hit.evidence_hint: All lions being bears can be possible; all tigers being wolves cannot when some tigers are bears and no bear is a wolf.

must_hit.point: An undefined subject-predicate pair may still be either-or if every diagram makes exactly one of the complementary conclusions true.
must_hit.evidence_hint: For doors/windows/roofs or cars/buses/trains, candidate picks Either I or II when the pair is complementary and exhaustive.

must_hit.point: Relying on one minimum-overlap diagram for Some is unsafe; extreme cases including complete overlap must be tested.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions checking full overlap so Some does not force Some-not.

probes: How do you decide whether All X being Y is a possibility, and how is that different from treating two conclusions as either-or?
Why must you test complete-overlap diagrams when the premises only say Some?

hints.1: Ask whether you need one workable diagram or truth in every diagram.
hints.2: For possibility, try to draw the claimed arrangement without breaking premises; for either-or, check complementary exhaustion.
hints.3: Lions-in-bears can work; all-tigers-wolves cannot; Some does not imply Some-not because complete overlap is allowed.

phases.goal: Apply Venn syllogism rules and set formulas to counting, three-set inclusion-exclusion, exactly-two, and min-max overlap.

must_hit.point: For 80 students with 45 Math, 50 Science, and 10 neither, union is 70, intersection is 25, and exactly one is 45.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses 80−10=70, then 45+50−intersection=70 ⇒ intersection 25, then exactly one =20+25=45 or |M|+|S|−2|∩|.

must_hit.point: Three-set inclusion-exclusion with 40, 50, 30 and pairwise 15, 10, 12 plus all-three 5 gives union 88, so none of 100 is 12.
Exactly two sports requires subtracting the all-three count from each pairwise intersection: 20−10, 15−10, 10−10 sum to 15.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate gets 10+5+0=15 after removing the triple from each pair.

must_hit.point: For 200 employees with 130 coffee and 110 tea, overlap is at most 110 and at least 40.
Minimum all-three passes among 100 with 80/75/70 passers is 25 by maximizing disjoint failures 20+25+30=75.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses failures 20, 25, 30, sums to 75, then 100−75=25.

probes: In a class of 80 with 45 Math, 50 Science, and 10 neither, how many like exactly one subject?
For 130 coffee and 110 tea drinkers among 200 employees, what are the min and max who drink both?

hints.1: Write the union from total minus neither, or bound overlap with min set size and the union ≤ total constraint.
hints.2: Two-set: |∪|=|A|+|B|−|∩|; exactly one = |A|+|B|−2|∩|; three-set add back the triple.
hints.3: Exactly one =45; coffee/tea overlap ranges from 40 to 110.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Definite must hold in every valid diagram; possibility only needs one valid diagram. Example: All lions being bears can be drawn, but all tigers being wolves cannot because bear-tigers are barred from wolves.

tradeoffs.topic: Complementary either-or pairs vs false Some/Some-not pairs
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Either-or uses Some A are B with No A is B, or All A are B with Some A are not B, when neither is individually definite and they exhaust cases. Some with Some-not is not either-or because both can be true together, so the answer may be Neither.

tradeoffs.topic: Maximum overlap vs minimum overlap in two sets
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Maximum overlap is the size of the smaller set (e.g. min(130,110)=110). Minimum overlap is forced by |A|+|B|−|∩| ≤ total (e.g. ≥40 when total is 200).

gotchas.trap: Treating Some A are B as implying Some A are not B.
gotchas.correction: In formal logic Some means at least one, possibly all. Test extreme cases including complete overlap; do not rely on a single minimum-overlap diagram.

gotchas.trap: Calling Some A are B and Some A are not B an either-or complementary pair.
gotchas.correction: Those are not mutually exclusive and do not exhaust a dichotomy. If neither follows definitely, the answer is Neither, not Either I or II.

gotchas.trap: Reading pairwise intersection counts as exactly-two without removing the all-three region.
gotchas.correction: Pairwise figures include the triple. Exactly two = each pairwise minus all-three, then sum those exclusive double regions.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an optional overlap is a definite conclusion.
gotchas.correction: If a circle can but need not meet another (e.g. Birds with Cats while overlapping Dogs), the Some conclusion does not follow; only relations forced in every diagram do.
